# Shifts of Address

*Chapter 7 of the proposed book. Research draft, 8 October 2026. Complete al-Fātiḥa and the local sequence 10:21–23, with an explicit reference map. Independent Arabic and scholarly review pending.*

Imagine hearing someone praise a person who is present. The speaker describes that person's generosity, then turns and says, “You have helped us.” The subject has not changed. The relationship enacted by the words has. Description has become address.

This ordinary possibility helps explain a feature that can initially puzzle readers of the Qur’an. A passage may move between speaking about someone and speaking to them, or between different grammatical presentations of a speaker. Arabic rhetorical discussion calls certain such turns *iltifāt*. Translating the term as “turning” preserves the image, but does not yet tell us which changes count or what they accomplish.

Our question is therefore more precise than whether the Qur’an changes pronouns. Where does a change occur? Does the referent remain the same? Has a quotation begun? What changes in the discourse at that point? An answer should make the reader better able to follow the passage, rather than merely attach a prestigious name to something unusual.

## Begin with the complete prayer

Al-Fātiḥa is short enough to read in full. These seven numbered verses follow the project's pinned Tanzil representation, including the basmala as 1:1. Other verse-numbering conventions require their own documentation. [ADR-01: text and representation](../data/manifest.json)

> بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ
>
> ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَـٰلَمِينَ
>
> ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ
>
> مَـٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ
>
> إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ
>
> ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَٰطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ
>
> صِرَٰطَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ

**An original working rendering:**

> In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Merciful.
>
> Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds,
>
> the All-Merciful, the Merciful,
>
> Master of the Day of Judgment.
>
> You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.
>
> Guide us on the straight path,
>
> the path of those You have favored, other than those under anger or those who have gone astray.

The last verse contains translation decisions that deserve a separate review. The Arabic construction for those under anger does not explicitly name an agent in that expression. This rendering preserves that restraint. Identifying particular historical groups is outside this chapter's argument.

Through verse 4, God is named and characterized. Verse 5 addresses Him. The same God who is praised becomes the “You” to whom worship and dependence are declared. The worshippers appear as the “we” of the verbs, and the next verse requests guidance for “us.” These are distinct relations within one prayer, not a succession of unrelated topics.

## A grammatical turn with a purpose

Al-Zamakhsharī explicitly asks why the wording turns from third-person presentation to direct address at 1:5. He connects the change with the preceding divine descriptions and the act of worship that follows. His explanation gives us a hypothesis about the sequence: the descriptions prepare the address. It does not supply experimental evidence about how every listener responds. [ADR-02: al-Zamakhsharī on 1:5](https://quran-tafsir.net/zamakhshary/sura1-aya5.html)

Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise connects the turn with the movement from praise toward supplication. That is a stronger local explanation than saying that any change prevents boredom. The request for guidance belongs naturally to direct address, and verse 5 makes the relationship explicit before the request arrives. [ADR-05: Ibn ʿĀshūr on 1:5](https://quran-tafsir.net/ashour/sura1-aya5.html)

Look at the arrangement through three related questions. Who is described? Who speaks within the prayer? To whom is the request directed? The answers make the turn intelligible. The prayer does not introduce a second deity at “You.” It changes how the same referent is presented. Nor does the first-person plural establish multiple authors of the Qur’an. It identifies the worshippers' represented voice within the prayer. A text's claimed ultimate source and a voice supplied for its readers are different questions.

There is another choice at the same point. The object expression *iyyāka* precedes each verb. Our “You alone” follows the exclusivity reading discussed by al-Zamakhsharī. Fronting and the change of person cooperate: worship and help are directed toward the one just praised. We should give each feature its share of the explanation rather than attributing everything to a pronoun change. [ADR-02: the fronted object](https://quran-tafsir.net/zamakhshary/sura1-aya5.html)

A teaching paraphrase makes the distinction easier to hear: “We worship God, and we ask God for help.” That wording retains the basic propositions but keeps describing a relationship. Another paraphrase begins, “You are Lord of the worlds,” and continues entirely in address. That retains directness but removes the transition from praise about God to commitment addressed to Him. Neither is a serious rival composition. They isolate one choice so that its function can be discussed.

The proposed achievement is coordination within a complete prayer. Description, commitment, dependence, and request occur in a compact sequence. A reader can accept that account and still ask whether an exceptional human writer could accomplish it. The grammatical explanation advances the literary inquiry; it does not bypass the question of origin.

## Read a journey through its aftermath

The next example requires more context. Qur’an 10:22 moves from addressing travelers to describing them. Its surrounding verses matter because the journey illustrates a larger contrast between distress, relief, and conduct after relief. The following is the complete local sequence 10:21–23, not a reading of all of Surah Yūnus. [ADR-01: unchanged Arabic](../data/manifest.json)

**10:21**

> وَإِذَآ أَذَقْنَا ٱلنَّاسَ رَحْمَةً مِّنۢ بَعْدِ ضَرَّآءَ مَسَّتْهُمْ إِذَا لَهُم مَّكْرٌ فِىٓ ءَايَاتِنَا ۚ قُلِ ٱللَّهُ أَسْرَعُ مَكْرًا ۚ إِنَّ رُسُلَنَا يَكْتُبُونَ مَا تَمْكُرُونَ

**10:22**

> هُوَ ٱلَّذِى يُسَيِّرُكُمْ فِى ٱلْبَرِّ وَٱلْبَحْرِ ۖ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا كُنتُمْ فِى ٱلْفُلْكِ وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم بِرِيحٍ طَيِّبَةٍ وَفَرِحُوا۟ بِهَا جَآءَتْهَا رِيحٌ عَاصِفٌ وَجَآءَهُمُ ٱلْمَوْجُ مِن كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَظَنُّوٓا۟ أَنَّهُمْ أُحِيطَ بِهِمْ ۙ دَعَوُا۟ ٱللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ ٱلدِّينَ لَئِنْ أَنجَيْتَنَا مِنْ هَـٰذِهِۦ لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلشَّـٰكِرِينَ

**10:23**

> فَلَمَّآ أَنجَىٰهُمْ إِذَا هُمْ يَبْغُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ ٱلْحَقِّ ۗ يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّمَا بَغْيُكُمْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُم ۖ مَّتَـٰعَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا ۖ ثُمَّ إِلَيْنَا مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَنُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ

**An original working rendering:**

> When We let people taste mercy after hardship has touched them, suddenly they scheme concerning Our signs. Say: “God is swifter in counter-planning. Our messengers record what you scheme.”
>
> He is the one who enables you to travel on land and sea. When you are in the ships, and they sail with them in a favorable wind, and they rejoice in it, a violent wind comes upon the ships, and waves come upon them from every place. They think they have been surrounded. They call upon God, making their devotion sincere to Him: “If You rescue us from this, we will surely be among the thankful.”
>
> Then, when He rescues them, suddenly they act wrongfully on earth without right. People, your wrongdoing bears upon yourselves. It is an enjoyment of the present life. Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.

Some English repetitions here are deliberate. The unusual “they sail with them” keeps the boats and their passengers distinguishable: the Arabic sailing verb has the boats as its subject, while the attached pronoun in *bihim* refers to the travelers. A smoother English translation could conceal the very relation being examined. The rendering of the short expression about worldly enjoyment in 10:23 is provisional and is not used to decide its disputed syntactic analysis.

## Find the turn, rather than every pronoun

The movement inside 10:22 begins with “you”: He enables **you** to travel; when **you** are in the ships. It then presents the same travelers as “them”: the ships sail with **them**, and **they** rejoice. Later **they** face danger and call for rescue.

Al-Qurṭubī identifies the change from address to third-person presentation and notes that this occurs in Arabic poetry as well as the Qur’an. That observation is essential to a fair argument. The device itself is available to human writers. Its presence cannot establish inimitability. [ADR-03: al-Qurṭubī on 10:22](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/qortobi/sura10-aya22.html)

Al-Zamakhsharī offers a more specific reading of its function here. He understands the move into third-person description as presenting the travelers' condition to others, inviting surprise and disapproval. This is an interpretation grounded in the passage's changing presentation and its moral aftermath. It is not a finding that actual readers necessarily experience a measurable increase in disapproval. [ADR-04: al-Zamakhsharī on 10:22](https://quran-tafsir.net/zamakhshary/sura10-aya22.html)

That reading becomes more persuasive when we keep verse 23 attached. Rescue is followed by renewed wrongdoing, and the vocative “People” leads into an admonition addressed to an audience. The story becomes a warning that hearers must consider in relation to themselves. We should not silently assume that every person addressed by this general vocative is numerically identical to the travelers described. Connecting an exemplifying group with a wider audience is a discourse relation, not automatically a same-referent pronoun substitution.

The plea inside 10:22 needs another distinction. “If You rescue us” is represented direct speech by the travelers. Its “You” addresses God, and its “us” identifies the people pleading. An English editor supplies quotation marks; the Arabic signals the prayer through the call upon God and the ensuing words. Crossing into that represented speech changes the speaking situation. Counting its pronouns as another instance of the same narrator's shift would mix different phenomena.

The nearby command “Say” in verse 21 also requires a speech-layer annotation. Our small inventory records it as context rather than using it to manufacture additional examples. This chapter examines selected transitions; it does not claim to catalogue every rhetorical turn in these verses.

## Make a reference map people can inspect

| Place | Grammatical presentation | Referent or voice | Immediate discourse role |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1:2–4 | God named and characterized | God | Praise and description |
| 1:5 | Second-person object, first-person plural verbs | God addressed by worshippers | Worship and dependence declared |
| 1:6–7 | Request and continued address | God addressed by worshippers | Guidance requested |
| 10:22, opening | Second-person plural | Travelers addressed | Entry into the situation |
| 10:22, sailing onward | Third-person plural for the passengers | Same travelers described | Their condition narrated |
| 10:22, rescue plea | Second-person singular and first-person plural within direct speech | God addressed by travelers | Promise made under distress |
| 10:23, aftermath | Third-person plural, then a general vocative and address | Rescued travelers; people addressed | Conduct exposed and warning extended |

The first two columns identify inspectable grammatical and reference proposals. The last column summarizes our interpretation. Keeping the columns distinct makes a disagreement useful: a reviewer might accept the grammar while proposing a different role for the turn.

The companion [annotation inventory](../analysis/address-map.json) links selected anchors to the unchanged corpus. Its [method note](../analysis/address-map.md) states the decisions; its [CSV table](../analysis/address-map.csv) can be inspected without specialized software. Extraction checks confirm that the anchors occur in their declared verses. They do not certify our reference assignments or prove the interpretation.

## Define the category before counting

There is no benefit in presenting an apparently precise total under an undefined category. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes a disagreement between the majority definition and al-Sakkākī's broader treatment. One requires an actual movement between presentations of the same referent; the other can include departure from the presentation expected in a situation. A case of self-address may consequently be included under one definition and excluded under another. [ADR-05: the definition discussion](https://quran-tafsir.net/ashour/sura1-aya5.html)

For this chapter's two selected comparison points, we use the narrower operational question: does the same referent change grammatical presentation within the same represented speech layer? A separate label records a quotation boundary or a move to a broader audience. These labels are editorial rules for a small inventory, not a resolution of the entire rhetorical tradition.

A simple formal notation helps keep those rules clear. Represent an annotated mention as a tuple *(r, p, s)*: referent, grammatical person, and speech layer. For a preselected pair of mentions, flag a person transition when *r* and *s* remain the same while *p* changes. We also allow a named referent in third-person presentation, following the classification Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly discusses. The flag says that a condition in the annotation rule has been met. It says nothing about beauty or origin.

The program evaluates two illustrative pairs: the divine description-to-address transition in al-Fātiḥa and the travelers' address-to-description transition in 10:22. Both receive the flag under the supplied annotations, in opposite directions. Two further pairs illustrate exclusion under this rule: a quotation boundary and the extension to a general audience. That is a transparent summary of selected examples, not an estimate of how often the Qur’an uses *iltifāt*. Choosing striking cases and then reporting their frequency as a general discovery would be circular.

## What the modern dispute asks us to examine

M. A. S. Abdel Haleem's 1992 article directly addresses grammatical shifts and their rhetorical purposes. Its publisher's opening extract contrasts a negative judgment attributed to Nöldeke with favorable Arabic critical accounts, then argues for examining the positions and functions of changes. That methodological demand is useful regardless of which literary evaluation a reader ultimately accepts. [ADR-06: publisher extract and article record](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0041977X00003621)

Our inspection is limited to that opening extract and bibliographic record. Full article access was unavailable in this research pass. We have not independently inspected Nöldeke's cited German discussion, and do not use the reported criticism as evidence of either hostility or incompetence. Nor do we borrow a complete classification or frequency total from an article whose body we have not read.

The productive dispute is about explanation. Does a proposed function fit the exact location? Would it fit equally well if the change happened elsewhere? Does the interpretation account for the surrounding passage? These questions can distinguish a supported reading from an explanation attached after the fact.

## A reader study that could disagree with us

A future study could ask whether readers recover the referents and speech layers correctly before asking them to rate literary effects. Those outcomes differ. Someone can follow a passage accurately and judge a turn unnecessary; someone can admire a passage while misidentifying its speakers.

Begin with independent Arabic annotation. Reviewers should mark referents, person, quotation boundaries, and uncertain cases under a written manual. Compare their annotations before adjudicating them. Report the actual disagreements and the decisions used to resolve them. Agreement after a group discussion is not an independent reliability estimate.

For readers, use complete passages and strong human-authored comparison texts. Document language proficiency, prior familiarity, and whether participants recognize the Qur’anic material. Familiarity may make recognition unavoidable; removing the title does not guarantee blinding. Ask comprehension questions whose answers are established independently of a preference for one formulation.

Carefully reviewed teaching variants could preserve referents while retaining a single person throughout a selected stretch. Another variant could move the transition. These interventions test a local explanation only if their grammar and naturalness are adequate. A clumsy rewrite gives the original an artificial advantage. Variants should therefore be assessed before the main experiment, and they should never be represented as independently excellent rival surahs.

Record comprehension, perceived coherence, and literary preference separately. Use uncertainty intervals for response rates and account for repeated judgments by the same reader and on the same passage. A percentage calculated from many answers by a few people is not the same evidence as that percentage from independent readers. Any model and primary outcome should be specified before the results are available.

No reviewers or readers have been recruited for this chapter. We report no agreement coefficient, comprehension advantage, memory benefit, or preference result. The map and formal rule organize the questions that a study could test; they do not stand in for that study.

## What this contributes to the larger argument

The two examples disclose different uses of a shared linguistic resource. Al-Fātiḥa moves from praise into direct commitment and petition. The sea journey moves from addressed participation into description, then carries its aftermath into admonition. A universal explanation such as “all shifts create intimacy” would fail to describe both well.

This is a useful advance in the inimitability inquiry because it gives a critic specific claims to examine. The argument can ask whether the changes serve their settings, whether the whole compositions coordinate multiple purposes, and how strong alternatives accomplish comparable work. Its strength must come from the quality of those explanations and comparisons, rather than from treating the name *iltifāt* as a certificate of supernatural authorship.

Our affirmative reading is that these turns are motivated parts of their local sequences. Establishing that much leaves the harder questions open: how sustained the achievement is, what human literature can match, and whether the cumulative evidence supports revelation. A turn in address deserves close attention. It also deserves a conclusion proportionate to what has been shown.
